scenes.title: Bots flood checkout.
scenes.caption: Excess traffic can exhaust shared capacity. Real shoppers face slow checkout or timeouts. Reject excess work before processing.

scenes.title: Limit the noisy caller.
scenes.caption: Illustrative rule: one caller sends eight requests. Five proceed and three receive 429 before checkout.

scenes.title: A window has a boundary.
scenes.caption: A fixed window allows five requests in [0,10). At t=5, that allowance is still exhausted.

scenes.title: Tokens refill gradually.
scenes.caption: Capacity 5. Refill 0.5 tokens per second. At t=5, an empty bucket has 2.5 tokens: two requests pass.

scenes.title: 429 means slow down.
scenes.caption: Retry-After explains when to try again. It does not reserve capacity or guarantee checkout success.

scenes.title: Choose the failure policy.
scenes.caption: Use trusted caller identity, atomic shared decisions, and an explicit plan for limiter-store outages.

socialHooks: When bots flood checkout, real customers pay the price in delays and errors. How can rate limiting help?
Why does a token bucket admit two requests after five seconds? Try the model.
Rate limiting protects capacity. It does not make payments idempotent.
